To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
CD4+ effectors, rather than cytolytic T lymphocytes, control the initial phase of EBV-induced B cell proliferation.
CD4+ effectors inhibit EBV-induced B cell proliferation.
CD4+ but no CD8+ T-cell effectors limit EBV-induced B cell proliferation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of B-cell proliferation in the context of EBV infection.
the role of T cells in the immune response to EBV.
understanding the role of the immune system in the control of EBV infection, and how this control is compromised in immunodeficient patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the early proliferative response of B cells to EBV infection is regulated in vitro by CD4+ T-cell effectors.
EBV-infected, activated, CD23+ B lymphocytes undergo a rapid proliferative burst in the absence of T-cell surveillance, which is prevented by CD4+ T-cell effectors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the early-phase proliferation of EBV-inflicted B cells is controlled by CD4+ effectors.
CD4+ effectors inhibit early-phase proliferation of activated B cells infected with EBV.
EBV infection induces B-cell proliferation, and CD4+ T-cell effectors inhibit this proliferation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CD4+ effektor cells can inhibit the proliferation of activated EBV-infected cells, and this effect is not mediated by cytokines, but by direct cell-cell interactions.
CD4+ cells are the main effectors of immune control of EBV infection.
EBV infection of B cells induces a proliferative response that is controlled by CD4+ T-cell effectors.
